1 # Design Tokens System for SaaS Applications 2 3 **Last updated: 2026-04-04** 4 5 A comprehensive guide to modern design tokens used across production SaaS applications. This document covers the complete token system powering Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, and Geist design systems. 6 7 --- 8 9 ## Overview 10 11 Design tokens are named entities that store visual design attributes—colors, spacing, typography, shadows, and more—defined once and reused everywhere. They enable: 12 - Consistent, scalable design systems 13 - Rapid theme switching (light/dark mode) 14 - Accessibility compliance (WCAG AA) 15 - Maintainability across large teams 16 17 The modern approach uses CSS variables as the foundation, with Tailwind CSS providing utilities on top. 18 19 --- 20 21 ## 1. Color System 22 23 ### 1.1 Semantic Color Naming 24 25 Modern SaaS design systems organize colors by **function** rather than appearance. This prevents mistakes (e.g., accidentally using green for a delete button) and enables global updates. 26 27 **Core semantic color roles:** 28 29 | Role | Purpose | Examples | 30 |------|---------|----------| 31 | `primary` | Main brand color, key actions | CTA buttons, links, primary navigation | 32 | `secondary` | Supporting brand color | Secondary buttons, accents | 33 | `accent` | Brand moments | Highlights, badges, onboarding | 34 | `success` | Positive outcomes | Success messages, growth indicators | 35 | `warning` | Caution states | Warnings, review-required states | 36 | `destructive` | Dangerous/irreversible actions | Delete buttons, error states | 37 | `info` | Informational content | Info badges, help text | 38 | `muted` | Secondary content | Disabled states, placeholders | 39 | `background` | Page/surface backgrounds | Body background, container fills | 40 | `foreground` | Text and primary content | Body text, icons on backgrounds | 41 42 **Foreground pairs:** 43 44 Every background token has a corresponding foreground token: 45 - `--background` + `--foreground` (page background) 46 - `--card` + `--card-foreground` (card surfaces) 47 - `--primary` + `--primary-foreground` (primary buttons) 48 - `--muted` + `--muted-foreground` (disabled/secondary) 49 50 ### 1.2 shadcn/ui CSS Variables (Light + Dark) 51 52 shadcn/ui provides a complete CSS variable system that works with CSS custom properties and Tailwind CSS. 53 54 **Light theme (`:root`):** 55 56 ```css 57 :root { 58 /* Backgrounds & Surfaces */ 59 --background: 0 0% 100%; /* White */ 60 --foreground: 0 0% 3.6%; /* Almost black */ 61 62 --card: 0 0% 100%; 63 --card-foreground: 0 0% 3.6%; 64 65 --popover: 0 0% 100%; 66 --popover-foreground: 0 0% 3.6%; 67 68 --muted: 0 0% 96.1%; /* Light gray */ 69 --muted-foreground: 0 0% 45.1%; /* Medium gray */ 70 71 /* Primary Color (Brand) */ 72 --primary: 0 0% 9%; /* Dark color by default */ 73 --primary-foreground: 0 0% 98%; /* White on primary */ 74 75 /* Secondary Color */ 76 --secondary: 0 0% 96.1%; 77 --secondary-foreground: 0 0% 9%; 78 79 /* Accent (Highlights) */ 80 --accent: 0 0% 9%; 81 --accent-foreground: 0 0% 98%; 82 83 /* Destructive (Delete, Error) */ 84 --destructive: 0 84.2% 60.2%; /* Red */ 85 --destructive-foreground: 0 0% 98%; 86 87 /* UI Elements */ 88 --border: 0 0% 89.8%; /* Light border */ 89 --input: 0 0% 89.8%; /* Input field background */ 90 --ring: 0 0% 3.6%; /* Focus ring color */ 91 92 /* Border Radius */ 93 --radius: 0.5rem; /* Default 8px */ 94 } 95 ``` 96 97 **Dark theme (`.dark`):** 98 99 ```css 100 .dark { 101 --background: 0 0% 3.6%; /* Almost black */ 102 --foreground: 0 0% 98%; /* Near white */ 103 104 --card: 0 0% 10%; /* Slightly lighter black */ 105 --card-foreground: 0 0% 98%; 106 107 --popover: 0 0% 3.6%; 108 --popover-foreground: 0 0% 98%; 109 110 --muted: 0 0% 14.9%; /* Dark gray */ 111 --muted-foreground: 0 0% 63.9%; /* Light gray */ 112 113 --primary: 0 0% 98%; /* Near white */ 114 --primary-foreground: 0 0% 9%; /* Dark on light primary */ 115 116 --secondary: 0 0% 14.9%; 117 --secondary-foreground: 0 0% 98%; 118 119 --accent: 0 0% 98%; 120 --accent-foreground: 0 0% 9%; 121 122 --destructive: 0 84.2% 60.2%; /* Red stays consistent */ 123 --destructive-foreground: 0 0% 10%; 124 125 --border: 0 0% 14.9%; /* Dark border */ 126 --input: 0 0% 14.9%; /* Dark input */ 127 --ring: 0 0% 83.3%; /* Light ring in dark mode */ 128 } 129 ``` 130 131 **Chart colors (for data visualization):** 132 133 ```css 134 :root { 135 --chart-1: 12 76% 61%; /* Blue */ 136 --chart-2: 173 58% 39%; /* Teal */ 137 --chart-3: 197 37% 24%; /* Navy */ 138 --chart-4: 43 74% 66%; /* Yellow */ 139 --chart-5: 27 87% 67%; /* Orange */ 140 } 141 142 .dark { 143 --chart-1: 210 70% 56%; /* Lighter blue for dark */ 144 --chart-2: 175 58% 54%; 145 --chart-3: 200 37% 54%; 146 --chart-4: 45 74% 75%; 147 --chart-5: 30 87% 75%; 148 } 149 ``` 150 151 ### 1.3 HSL-Based Color System 152 153 Modern design systems use HSL (Hue, Saturation, Lightness) instead of hex because it's easier to reason about colors programmatically. 154 155 **HSL Structure:** 156 - **Hue** (0-360°): The color itself (red=0, yellow=60, green=120, cyan=180, blue=240, magenta=300) 157 - **Saturation** (0-100%): Intensity of color (0%=gray, 100%=vivid) 158 - **Lightness** (0-100%): Brightness (0%=black, 50%=normal, 100%=white) 159 160 **Example: Creating a brand color scale from primary blue (210°):** 161 162 ```css 163 /* Light mode */ 164 --blue-50: 210 100% 97%; /* Nearly white with hint of blue */ 165 --blue-100: 210 100% 94%; 166 --blue-200: 210 98% 88%; 167 --blue-300: 210 96% 80%; 168 --blue-400: 210 94% 70%; 169 --blue-500: 210 91% 60%; /* Primary blue */ 170 --blue-600: 210 85% 50%; 171 --blue-700: 210 80% 40%; /* Darker for text on light BG */ 172 --blue-800: 210 75% 30%; 173 --blue-900: 210 70% 15%; /* Very dark */ 174 175 /* Dark mode: shift lightness up, keep hue/saturation similar */ 176 --blue-50: 210 100% 20%; /* Darkish, subtle */ 177 --blue-500: 210 91% 65%; /* Brighter in dark mode */ 178 --blue-700: 210 80% 55%; /* Adjusted for dark mode readability */ 179 ``` 180 181 ### 1.4 Radix Colors System 182 183 Radix Themes provides ~30 pre-tuned color scales, each with light, dark, and alpha variants. Each scale has 12 steps designed for specific uses: 184 185 **Steps 1-3:** Backgrounds (subtle containers) 186 **Steps 4-6:** Interactive/hover states 187 **Steps 7-8:** Borders 188 **Steps 9-10:** Solid interactive elements 189 **Steps 11-12:** High-contrast text 190 191 Available colors: Gray, Gold, Bronze, Brown, Yellow, Amber, Orange, Tomato, Red, Ruby, Crimson, Pink, Plum, Purple, Violet, Iris, Indigo, Blue, Cyan, Teal, Jade, Green, Grass, Lime, Mint, Sky. 192 193 ### 1.5 Color Contrast & Accessibility 194 195 **WCAG AA Standards (minimum):** 196 197 | Content Type | Ratio | Example | 198 |--------------|-------|---------| 199 | Normal text (< 18px) | 4.5:1 | Black text on white background | 200 | Large text (≥ 18pt or ≥ 14pt bold) | 3:1 | Larger heading with slightly lower contrast | 201 | UI components & icons | 3:1 | Button borders, icon against background | 202 203 **Practical approach:** 204 205 1. Use a contrast checker tool (e.g., [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/)) 206 2. Test both light and dark modes 207 3. Test with real text/icons, not just color blocks 208 4. Avoid pure black (#000000) on pure white (#FFFFFF) in dark mode—use off-black/off-white instead 209 210 **Common accessible pairings:** 211 - Dark gray (#424242) text on white background: 9.3:1 212 - White text on dark blue (#003366): 5.5:1 213 - Dark gray text on light gray (#f5f5f5): 7.6:1 214 215 ### 1.6 Neutral Gray Scales 216 217 Most SaaS apps need multiple neutral scales for flexibility: 218 219 | Scale | Use Case | Saturation | 220 |-------|----------|-----------| 221 | **Zinc** | Default, most common | 0% (pure gray) | 222 | **Slate** | Softer, slightly blue-shifted | 2-3% blue | 223 | **Gray** | Generic fallback | Minimal saturation | 224 | **Stone** | Warm, slightly brown-shifted | 1-2% warm | 225 226 **Zinc scale (most common):** 227 ``` 228 zinc-50: #fafafa (almost white) 229 zinc-100: #f4f4f5 230 zinc-200: #e4e4e7 231 zinc-300: #d4d4d8 232 zinc-400: #a1a1aa (medium gray, good for placeholders) 233 zinc-500: #71717a 234 zinc-600: #52525b 235 zinc-700: #3f3f46 (good for body text) 236 zinc-800: #27272a 237 zinc-900: #18181b (almost black) 238 ``` 239 240 ### 1.7 Data Visualization Colors 241 242 **Categorical palette (≤ 7 colors for distinct categories):** 243 ```css 244 --vis-cat-1: 12 76% 61%; /* Blue */ 245 --vis-cat-2: 173 58% 39%; /* Teal */ 246 --vis-cat-3: 197 37% 24%; /* Navy */ 247 --vis-cat-4: 43 74% 66%; /* Yellow */ 248 --vis-cat-5: 27 87% 67%; /* Orange */ 249 --vis-cat-6: 0 84% 60%; /* Red */ 250 --vis-cat-7: 280 85% 60%; /* Purple */ 251 ``` 252 253 **Sequential palette (for ordered data like time/intensity):** 254 ```css 255 --vis-seq-1: 210 100% 95%; /* Light (low value) */ 256 --vis-seq-2: 210 95% 85%; 257 --vis-seq-3: 210 90% 70%; 258 --vis-seq-4: 210 85% 50%; 259 --vis-seq-5: 210 80% 35%; 260 --vis-seq-6: 210 75% 20%; /* Dark (high value) */ 261 ``` 262 263 **Diverging palette (for opposing values, e.g., -50 to +50):** 264 ```css 265 --vis-div-neg-3: 10 86% 60%; /* Red (negative) */ 266 --vis-div-neg-2: 10 60% 75%; 267 --vis-div-neg-1: 10 30% 90%; 268 --vis-div-mid: 0 0% 95%; /* Neutral */ 269 --vis-div-pos-1: 200 30% 90%; 270 --vis-div-pos-2: 200 60% 75%; 271 --vis-div-pos-3: 200 86% 60%; /* Blue (positive) */ 272 ``` 273 274 **Note:** Use [ColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org/) for pre-tested, colorblind-safe palettes. 275 276 --- 277 278 ## 2. Spacing System 279 280 ### 2.1 4px Grid Foundation 281 282 One unit in Tailwind = 0.25rem = 4px (assuming 16px browser default). 283 284 **Benefits:** 285 - Provides granularity (4px steps vs. 8px steps) 286 - Aligns with modern UI expectations 287 - Works well on mobile (even spacing feels natural) 288 289 ### 2.2 Default Spacing Scale 290 291 ``` 292 0 = 0px 293 px = 1px (for borders) 294 0.5 = 2px 295 1 = 4px [1 unit] 296 1.5 = 6px 297 2 = 8px [2 units, minimum spacing] 298 2.5 = 10px 299 3 = 12px [3 units, common gap] 300 3.5 = 14px 301 4 = 16px [4 units, common padding] 302 5 = 20px 303 6 = 24px [6 units, card padding] 304 7 = 28px 305 8 = 32px [8 units, large spacing] 306 9 = 36px 307 10 = 40px 308 12 = 48px [12 units, section spacing] 309 14 = 56px 310 16 = 64px [16 units, hero spacing] 311 20 = 80px 312 24 = 96px 313 28 = 112px 314 32 = 128px 315 36 = 144px 316 40 = 160px 317 44 = 176px 318 48 = 192px 319 52 = 208px 320 56 = 224px 321 60 = 240px 322 64 = 256px 323 72 = 288px 324 80 = 320px 325 96 = 384px 326 ``` 327 328 ### 2.3 Component Spacing Rules 329 330 **Padding (internal spacing inside components):** 331 - Buttons: `p-2` (8px) or `p-2.5` (10px) 332 - Input fields: `p-2` to `p-3` (8-12px) 333 - Card content: `p-6` (24px) 334 - Large sections: `p-8` to `p-12` (32-48px) 335 336 **Margin/Gap (external spacing):** 337 - Form field vertical gap: `gap-4` (16px) 338 - Card list gap: `gap-6` (24px) 339 - Section margin: `my-8` to `my-12` (32-48px) 340 - Between major sections: `my-16` (64px) 341 342 **Container max-widths (Tailwind defaults):** 343 ``` 344 sm: 640px (mobile optimization) 345 md: 768px (tablet) 346 lg: 1024px (desktop) 347 xl: 1280px (wide desktop) 348 2xl: 1536px (ultra-wide) 349 ``` 350 351 --- 352 353 ## 3. Typography 354 355 ### 3.1 Font Stack 356 357 **Recommended primary font: Inter** 358 - Purpose: Body text and UI 359 - Reason: Specifically designed for screens, high legibility, variable font support 360 - Fallback chain: `Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif` 361 362 **Secondary font: Geist Mono (code)** 363 - Purpose: Code blocks, monospace content 364 - Fallback: `ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Consolas, 'Courier New', monospace` 365 366 ### 3.2 Type Scale 367 368 Using a 1.25x modular scale (16px base): 369 370 ```css 371 /* Light theme */ 372 :root { 373 --text-xs: 0.75rem / 1rem; /* 12px / 16px line-height */ 374 --text-sm: 0.875rem / 1.25rem; /* 14px / 20px */ 375 --text-base: 1rem / 1.5rem; /* 16px / 24px */ 376 --text-lg: 1.125rem / 1.75rem; /* 18px / 28px */ 377 --text-xl: 1.25rem / 1.75rem; /* 20px / 28px */ 378 --text-2xl: 1.5rem / 2rem; /* 24px / 32px */ 379 --text-3xl: 1.875rem / 2.25rem; /* 30px / 36px */ 380 --text-4xl: 2.25rem / 2.5rem; /* 36px / 40px */ 381 --text-5xl: 3rem / 1.2; /* 48px / responsive */ 382 --text-6xl: 3.75rem / 1; /* 60px / no line-height */ 383 --text-7xl: 4.5rem / 1; /* 72px */ 384 --text-8xl: 6rem / 1; /* 96px */ 385 --text-9xl: 8rem / 1; /* 128px */ 386 } 387 ``` 388 389 **Tailwind classes:** 390 ```html 391 392

# Deep Dive: Color System Design for SaaS

**Last updated: 2026-04-04**

A comprehensive guide to designing, implementing, and maintaining color systems in production SaaS applications. This document focuses on color-specific patterns, theme switching, accessibility, and brand integration.

---

## Overview

A mature SaaS color system requires:
1. **Brand color selection** that works in light and dark modes
2. **CSS variable architecture** for switching themes
3. **Semantic color naming** (what colors mean, not what they are)
4. **Accessibility testing** (WCAG AA compliance)
5. **Data visualization palettes** (charts, graphs, analytics)
6. **Dark mode variants** that preserve intent, not just invert colors

---

## 1. Brand Color Selection Guide

### 1.1 Choosing Your Primary Brand Color

The primary color should:
- **Evoke the right emotion** for your market (trust, innovation, growth, etc.)
- **Work in both light and dark modes** without adjustment
- **Pass WCAG AA contrast** with white text (4.5:1 minimum)
- **Differentiate from competitors** in your space
- **Be testable on different screens** and devices

**Emotion-to-Color Mapping (for SaaS):**

| Emotion | Color | Common SaaS Examples |
|---------|-------|----------------------|
| Trust, Security | Blue | Stripe, Slack, GitHub |
| Growth, Energy | Green | Notion, Webflow, Supabase |
| Innovation, Tech | Purple | Twitch, Discord, OpenAI |
| Urgency, Action | Orange | Vercel, Shopify, GitLab |
| Premium, Luxury | Dark Gray/Black | Apple, Figma |
| Community, Fun | Vibrant Rainbow | Zapier, Figma (secondary) |

### 1.2 Testing Your Brand Color

Before finalizing, test your color:

**1. Contrast ratio (text on brand color background):**
```
Primary blue (#0066CC) on white: 5.1:1 ✓ (passes WCAG AA)
Primary blue on light gray: 4.8:1 ✓ (passes WCAG AA)
Primary blue on dark background: may fail—need adjustment for dark mode
```

**2. Light mode appearance:**
```
Primary: #0066CC (bright, vivid)
Text on primary: white (#FFFFFF)
Hover state: #0052A3 (darker shade)
Active state: #003D7A (even darker)
```

**3. Dark mode appearance (important!):**
Your light mode brand color will NOT work in dark mode. Adjust:
- Increase lightness (move toward white)
- Maintain hue (same color family)
- Reduce saturation slightly (less vivid)

```
Light mode primary: #0066CC (HSL: 210, 100%, 40%)
Dark mode primary: #60A5FA (HSL: 210, 96%, 65%)  [Much lighter]
Dark mode hover: #93C5FD (HSL: 210, 97%, 75%)    [Even lighter]
```

### 1.3 Creating a Brand Color Scale

From your primary color, generate 10+ variations for flexibility.

**Using HSL adjustment (recommended):**

```
Primary hue: 210° (blue)
Primary saturation: 100%

Light mode scale (decrease lightness):
50:   HSL(210, 100%, 97%)  #E0F2FE  ← Use for very subtle backgrounds
100:  HSL(210, 100%, 94%)  #BFE3FE
200:  HSL(210, 100%, 88%)  #7DD3FC
300:  HSL(210, 100%, 80%)  #38BDF8
400:  HSL(210, 100%, 70%)  #0EA5E9
500:  HSL(210, 100%, 60%)  #0284C7  ← Secondary action
600:  HSL(210, 100%, 50%)  #0066CC  ← Primary (YOUR BRAND COLOR)
700:  HSL(210, 100%, 40%)  #0052A3  ← Hover/darker
800:  HSL(210, 100%, 30%)  #003D7A
900:  HSL(210, 100%, 15%)  #001F3F  ← Darkest, use for text

Dark mode scale (different approach—adjust for dark BG):
50:   HSL(210, 100%, 25%)  #0C4A6E  ← Dark mode background tint
100:  HSL(210, 100%, 30%)  #082F49
200:  HSL(210, 100%, 40%)  #0C3D66
300:  HSL(210, 100%, 55%)  #0B7FA0  ← Base dark mode primary
400:  HSL(210, 96%, 65%)   #60A5FA
500:  HSL(210, 98%, 75%)   #93C5FD  ← Hover in dark mode
600:  HSL(210, 100%, 85%)  #BFE3FE
```

### 1.4 Testing Multiple Screens

**Create a test UI with your brand color:**
```
✓ White text on brand color (normal text)
✓ Brand colored buttons on white background
✓ Brand colored links in paragraphs
✓ Brand colored borders on cards
✓ Brand colored hover states
✓ All above on dark mode background
```

Test on:
- Desktop monitors (different calibrations)
- Mobile phones (different screen technologies)
- Tablets
- E-ink readers (if applicable)

---

## 2. CSS Variable Architecture for Theming

### 2.1 Three-Layer Token System

**Layer 1: Primitive Tokens (Raw Colors)**
Direct hex/HSL values, rarely referenced in code:
```css
--primitive-blue-50: hsl(210 100% 97%);
--primitive-blue-500: hsl(210 100% 60%);
--primitive-blue-900: hsl(210 100% 15%);
```

**Layer 2: Semantic Tokens (Intent-Based)**
Describe what the color means:
```css
--color-primary: var(--primitive-blue-600);
--color-primary-foreground: white;
--color-success: hsl(120 100% 40%);
--color-error: hsl(0 100% 50%);
--color-warning: hsl(40 100% 50%);
```

# Motion & Animation Design Guide for SaaS

**Last updated:** 2026-04-04

---

## Table of Contents

1. [Motion Principles](#motion-principles)
2. [Duration Scale](#duration-scale)
3. [Easing Functions](#easing-functions)
4. [Micro-Interactions](#micro-interactions)
5. [Framer Motion Patterns](#framer-motion-patterns)
6. [Tailwind Animation Classes](#tailwind-animation-classes)
7. [Accessibility](#accessibility)
8. [Performance Rules](#performance-rules)
9. [When NOT to Animate](#when-not-to-animate)

---

## Motion Principles

### Core Tenets

Motion in SaaS applications should follow four principles:

1. **Purposeful** — Every animation guides attention, clarifies hierarchy, or communicates state. Remove animations that exist only for aesthetics.
2. **Fast** — Animations in the 150-300ms range feel responsive and keep users in flow. Slower animations interrupt.
3. **Consistent** — Use the same easing curves across the entire application. Consistency builds trust and reduces cognitive load.
4. **Accessible** — Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Color changes and opacity shifts can remain; transforms should be removed for users who prefer reduced motion.

### Why Motion Matters in SaaS

Thoughtful micro-interactions reduce frustration, confirm system responses, and make the product feel alive and polished. Research shows that adding progress bars during onboarding can boost activation rates by up to 47%.

---

## Duration Scale

Use this timing scale consistently across your app:

| Duration | Use Case | Examples |
|----------|----------|----------|
| **Instant (0ms)** | Immediate visual feedback, no perceptible delay | Color changes, opacity micro-shifts on hover |
| **Fast (100-150ms)** | Quick interactive responses | Hover states, focus rings, tooltip fade-in, button color shift |
| **Normal (200-250ms)** | Standard state changes | Toggle switches, tab content switch, dropdown open/close |
| **Slow (300-400ms)** | Deliberate entrance effects | Modal backdrop fade, drawer slide, sheet overlay |
| **Deliberate (500ms+)** | Page transitions, onboarding sequences | Page exit/enter, carousel slide, stepper progression |

**Rationale:** Users perceive 100-400ms as responsive and immediate. Animations faster than 100ms often feel janky; slower than 400ms feel sluggish unless intentional (like page transitions).

---

## Easing Functions

Easing controls the acceleration/deceleration of motion. Choose the right easing for the direction of movement.

### CSS Easing Values

```css
/* ease-out: Fast start, gentle stop — USE FOR ENTERING ELEMENTS */
cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)

/* ease-in: Gentle start, fast finish — USE FOR EXITING ELEMENTS */
cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)

/* ease-in-out: Symmetric acceleration — USE FOR POSITION CHANGES */
cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)

/* ease-linear: Constant velocity — USE FOR PROGRESS, LOADING */
cubic-bezier(0, 0, 1, 1)
```

### Spring Easing (Framer Motion / Motion Library)

Spring animations mimic real-world physics and feel natural. Use for interactive, gesture-driven animations:

```typescript
// Standard spring (stiffness, damping, mass)
const springConfig = {
  stiffness: 400,    // How "bouncy" (higher = faster)
  damping: 30,       // How much resistance (higher = less bounce)
  mass: 1            // Inertia (affects overshoot)
}

// Snappy spring (faster, less bounce)
const snappy = {
  stiffness: 500,
  damping: 40,
  mass: 1
}

// Bouncy spring (slower, more playful)
const bouncy = {
  stiffness: 300,
  damping: 15,
  mass: 0.8
}
```
